newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - France to curb deficit but 3.0 pct unlikely.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - France to curb deficit but 3.0 pct unlikely.

text.p: French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn on Thursday said the public deficit could be significantly higher than forecast this year and the government would take action if needed to curb it.

But he suggested that it would not take the kind of drastic measures which might be needed to cut the deficit to precisely 3.0 percent of gross domestic product, the target fixed by its main partner Germany to qualify for European monetary union.
"The target will be defined according to what the economy can bear," he told a news conference. "We have to be able to reduce this deficit by a few decimal points."
Strauss-Kahn declined to forecast a figure for the deficit/GDP ratio this year, which he said must await the results of an independent audit of public finances due to be announced on July 21.

But he noted forecasts ranged between 3.4 percent, predicted by conservative parliamentarian and budget expert Philippe Auberger on Wednesday, and 3.8 percent, predicted by ministry officials before the June 1 parliamentary election.
"One can fear it will be more (than Auberger says). One can hope he is right," Strauss-Kahn said.
The previous centre-right government had targeted a deficit/GDP ratio of 3.0 percent in the 1997 Finance Act.
"The expectation is that the audit will show a deficit significantly higher than forecast," Strauss-Kahn said.

He added, however, that the trend over recent years showed the deficit falling by around 0.6 percentage points each year -- with the exception of this year, when revenues had fallen well short of expectations.

This should mean France would be able to continue cutting its deficit next year to meet European monetary union constraints, which seek to limit the deficit to three percent of GDP both before and after the launch of the new euro.

"If Monsieur Auberger is right, which I would like, and the deficit shown (by the audit) is 3.4 percent, it will undoubtedly be very easy, without making major leaps, to fall more or less into line," he said.
